content.summary_of_the_paper:
The paper describes a DETR-like transformer architecture for monocular 3D object detection. Depth-aware encodings are introduced for object queries, from a categorical depth prediction network. This network does not require any additional training information (apart from the 3D bounding boxes). The depth prediction network is trained using 3D planar (average depth) labels for each 3D object.
SoTA results are achieved on the KITTI dataset.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
The paper uses depth information to improve the expressiveness of a DETR-inspired transformer architecture, with convincing ablation studies and experimental results.

Weaknesses:
-The name of the paper, monoDETR is very similar to the Huang et. al. 2022 paper monoDTR. Maybe pick a better name?
-The conversion of the foreground depth map to the depth positional encoding is not clear. Please explain this better.
-Depth output resolution (depth bin resolution) is 1m. How did you decide this? Is this not going to affect the limit of the final accuracy of the bounding boxes?
-How are the object queries learnt? Are they in 2D image space or in 3D camera coordinate space? 
-The multi-view extension is not clearly explained (section 3.3). Don’t you need cameras extrinsics / [R,t] between cameras? How are the 3D reference points initialized for the object queries?
-Figure 3 caption typo: ‘learnbale’ should be learnable.
-A5 Monocular KITTI experiments: Doesn’t random cropping of the image affect depth estimation?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper is fairly well written, except for the generation of the depth positional encodings, which needs more explanation. Code has been provided, but I have not tried to reproduce it.
content.summary_of_the_review: A DETR-like transformer architecture with depth-image-enriched encodings is used for SoTA results on monocular 3D object detection. A monocular depth estimation network is used (without the requirement of dense image depth labels) for enriching the object queries in the transformer and making it learn inter-object geometric relationships. Ablation studies show the significance of the design choices of the network.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes to exploit box-level depth cues via depth-guided transformer in monocular 3D object detection. Based on DETR-style pipeline, the authors use object-wise depth labels to train an extra depth predictor, the intermediate depth feature of which is first enhanced by the depth encoder and then quired by object queries in the decoder. In addition, a depth positional encoding is designed to facilitate the capture of scene-level depth cues in the decoder. Extensive ablations on KITTI and nuScenes demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
a)	The use of object-wise depth labels without extra data is interesting.
b)	The design of depth-cross-attention in the object detection decoder is reasonable.

Weakness:
The main concerns are the novelty and contribution of the paper, which are not explained well. MonoDTR(CVPR2022) and PETR(ECCV2022)(or say PETRv2) are two works highly related to this work but not discussed or cited appropriately.
a)	Depth modules: MonoDTR:
Depth Positional Encoding via learnable depth prototypes, which plays a non-trivial role in depth decoder(Table 3), is first proposed in MonoDTR rather than this work. In this work, the authors only make minimal modifications to the original depth PE yet not cited MonoDTR in Method properly.
The authors indicate one two drawbacks of MonoDTR are: first, extra label of depth; second, the use of anchors and nms caused by center-based detection head. So they simply replace the former with box-level depth label and the later with detr-style head (see below).

b)	Detection decoder: PETR(PETRv2)
PETR is the first work to adapt DETR-style detection pipeline to vision-based 3D object detection, although it is a multi-camera-based algorithm, it can be degraded to monocular 3D object detection very easily. In fact, I think this work is an incremental work of PETR(PETRv2) with depth-related modules. However, there is only one experiment compared with PETRv2 on nuScenes val set and the performance gain is small.

Base on above facts, I think the contributions of this work are: 1) the utilization of box-level depth label; 2) depth-cross-attention in DETR head. Following experiments should be added to support the contributions:
i.	Performance comparison with PETRv2 on nuScenes test set. Please use the same setting(loss func, data aug, temporal information, etc) as PETRv2 except for modules related to depth. 
ii.	Comparison with depth-module of MonoDTR on KITTI. Please report the results of MonoDTR+ head proposed in this work without depth-cross-attention / the proposed model under object-wise depth label / dense depth label. This experiment is designed to show if the proposed depth-module only works well under weak depth supervision and if so, please explain it.
iii.	Please report the inference speed of the proposed method and compared it with that of MonoDTR on KITTI and that of PETRv2 on nuScenes. It seems extra visual encoder, depth encoder and global depth across-attention will result in extra inference time compared with PETRv2. (It is suggested to list the latency of each module as BEVFormer, cause image backbone seems to cost most of time).
content.summary_of_the_review: The authors do not clarify their contributions and do not discuss the most related works appropriately. Although there is some novelty, the authors need to add more experiment to support it.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
This paper presents Monocular Detection with a depth-guided Transformer (MonoDETR), a monocular 3D object detection method based on the transformer architecture. MonoDETR builds upon the general architecture of DETR, a transformer-based monocular 2D object detector, and extends it to a monocular 3D object detector. In particular, MonoDETR incorporates object depth information by predicting object-level depth maps from features that encode depth cues. Then these features are attended by the learned object queries using cross-attentions (depth-guided attentions) followed by self-attentions and cross-attentions between the query features and image features. Finally, the query features are used for predicting per-object properties with MLPs. The authors also show how to extend MonoDETR to MonoDETR-MV for multiple-view image inputs.
The experiments show that MonoDETR achieved state-of-the-art monocular 3D object detection on KITTI in the car category.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
### Strength
**S1**. The paper is well-written and one can follow it smoothly.

**S2**. The author proposed a depth-guided transformer decoder. Specifically, MonoDETR learns $N$ object queries (similar to DETR) which attend the depth-aware features (the features which predict the depth) using cross-attention, followed by self-attentions blocks. Then the query features cross-attend the image appearance features followed by self-attentions blocks. This way, the query features incorporate both depth-aware features and appearance features.

**S3**. MonoDETR achieves state-of-the-art results on the KITTI car benchmark using only monocular images as the inputs.

**S4**. The authors also provide a way to extend MonoDETR to a multi-view method (MonoDETR-MV) which also achieves competitive mAP and NDS on the nuScenes dataset.

**S5**. The authors conducted thorough ablation studies on the design of the network architecture including the depth-guided transformer components, the depth encoder components, the depth-guided decoder, and the depth positional encodings. In the supplementary materials, the authors further provide the ablation studies on the depth discretization method which is used to supervise depth estimation, bipartite matching, and the number of blocks for the visual encoder and depth encoder, as well as the number of channels of the feed-forward networks.

---
---

### Weaknesses
**W1**. The difference and relation to MonoDTR are not clearly stated. In fact, the general network architecture design and the key ingredient that uses depth as another source of supervision to learn depth-aware features are similar to MonoDTR and I suggest the authors clearly discuss the difference with MonoDTR in the paper. Architecture-wise, the major difference is that this work, MonoDETR, uses learned queries to get the final predictions while MonoDTR avoids such design on purpose: "*We propose utilizing the depth-aware features as the input of the decoder instead of learnable embeddings (object query), which is different from the common usage in previous encoder-decoder vision transformer works. The main reason is that, in the monocular 3D object detection task, the camera views at near and far distances often cause significant changes in object scale due to the perspective projection. It makes the simple learnable embedding hard to fully represent the object’s property and handle complex scale variant situations.*" What is your argument to make use of the object query design and why in the MonoDETR case this design is preferred?

**W2**. The loss functions are not discussed in the main paper at all. The loss functions are explained in the supplementary materials without mentioning in the main paper. First, as the loss function design is not trivial -- 8 loss terms in total if I'm not mistaken, it's better to be discussed in the main paper. More importantly, although there are a lot of loss terms, no ablation studies on the loss function are conducted. Some loss terms seem to play important roles: 1) $L_{xy3D}$. This term sets a clear difference to the center-guided method like MonoDTR. 2) $d_{pred}$. This loss term contains 3 sources of depth and also uncertainty prediction. It's better to know how important it is to include each depth source as well as the uncertainty estimation. 

**W3**. The state-of-the-art result on KITTI is a little bit overstated. In fact, MonoDETR achieves state-of-the-art results in the *car* category on KITTI. The results of *pedestrian* and *cyclist* categories still fall behind MonoDTR. However, the authors state that they achieve state-of-the-art results on KITTI generally in the abstract and introduction sections.

**W4**. I don't get why in practice this method would not need dense depth labels. Although the proposed loss formulation does not need dense depth directly, to get the object-level depth or the 3D bounding box annotations the dataset needs to have dense depth labels anyways. Therefore, I don't see this as a very meaningful advantage of the method although the authors claim it like "*MonoDETR achieves state-of-the-art and requires no extra dense depth annotations*".
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: This paper contains some interesting insights, in particular, on the design of the depth-guided transformer decoder, although it's not a significant novelty. The authors provide the code anonymously, which is very good for reproducibility.
content.summary_of_the_review: Given the weaknesses I stated above, especially about the loss function ablations and the discussion about MonoDTR, I would not accept that paper as it is. However, I'm looking forward to the authors' response and making the final decision based on that.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
The paper proposes a method for 3D object detection from monocular images.
It uses a transformer based neural network architecture that explicitly encodes depth and visual appearance into two separate embeddings, using an auxiliary loss predicting per-pixel labels to train the depth-based embedding. The core intuition behind this methods is to use depth cues to aggregate information from the relevant portions of the whole images, unlike traditional methods that typically aggregate information only from the pixels surrounding the centre of the predicted model.
The main contribution of the paper is to use embeddings that explicitly encode depth information to allow capturing interactions between objects at different depths in the scene, and an architecture that fuses both visual and depth embeddings.
The method is evaluated on standard benchmarks for monocular depth prediction (KITTI), achieving state-of-the-art performance. It is also evaluated in a multi view-setting on nuScenes, also achieving state-of-the-art.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
1) The intuitions behind the work are interesting, in particular the use of explicit depth cues to reason more holistically at a scene level compared to appearance-based only, or object-centric methods
2) The results are convincing, and performance achieves state-of-the-art on both monocular 3D object detection (on Kitti), and from multi-view (on nuscenes). 
3) Providing anonymised source code is valuable for reproducibility

Weaknesses:
1) The novelty seems incremental with respect to MonoDtr by Huang et al. (CVPR 2022). To the best of my understanding, the main differences are the use of object queries for adaptive feature aggregation (which is also not an original contribution of this paper, as this was introduced in DETR in a 2D setting),  and the reliance on less dense depth supervision
2) I was surprised that the delta between this submission and MonoDtr (the most relevant related work) is explained only briefly in the results section. I would have explained a thorough discussion of the differences between the submission and this paper
Learning Auxiliary Monocular Contexts Helps Monocular 3D Object Detection by Liu et al
3) The clarity of the exposition is often not sufficient to understand some important points of the paper. For example, I could understand some sentence only at an intuitive level, such us: "By the global self-attention mechanism, the depth encoder explores long-range dependencies of depth values from different foreground areas, which provides non-local geometric cues of the stereo space and interacts depth features among objects with long distances." or "By this, one query can know what boxes would other queries are going to predict and implicitly prevent duplicate boxes".  This is particularly problematic in the ablative analysis section (4.3): I could not understand and would not be able to reproduce seemingly important baselines like "w/o Depth-guided Trans." and " "w/o Transformer".
4) To me it remains unclear the extent to which  this is a beneficial (don't the sparse ground-truth depth label still require LIDAR data to be generated?). Is overall performance better when using sparse depth labels?

Minor suggestions/typos/missing citations:
1) In Table 2, on the right hand side, the best performing method is not highlighted in bold
2) Please cite: "Learning Auxiliary Monocular Contexts Helps Monocular 3D Object Detection" from Liu et al. this seems to be the current state-of-the-art on monocular 3D object dection ok Kitti
3) A few times Kitti is spelled incorrectly (KIITI)
4) "instead of using sinusoidal functions as others" --> add relevant reference
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity: In my opinion, the Clarity of the exposition does not meet the bar for acceptance. For example I could not understand how the baselines used in the ablative analysis section (4.3) work. 

Novelty: The novelty seems incremental with previous work, in particular with respect to MonoDtr by Huang et al. (CVPR 2022). To the best of my understanding, the main differences are the use of object queries for adaptive feature aggregation (which is also not an original contribution of this paper, as this was introduced in DETR in a 2D setting),  and the reliance on less dense depth supervision (to me it remains unclear the extent to which  this is a beneficial: don't the sparse ground-truth depth label still require LIDAR data to be generated)? This could caused in part by insufficient clarity: teasing out the key contributions with respect to MonoDtr from the text is not straightforward

Reproducibility: Based on the text, too many details are missing or not clear enough. However, this is mitigated by the authors producing anonymised source code
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper has some interesting intuition in the field of monocular 3D object detection, in particular the use of explicit depth cues to reason more holistically at a scene level compared to appearance-based only, or object-centric methods. Results are also convincing, achieving state-of-the-art on KITTI. However, the novelty of the contributions is in my opinion too incremental with respect to MonoDTR, and the difference between the submission and MonoDTR is not discuss in enough detail. The quality of exposition is in my opinion not sufficient for acceptance, for example I could not understand how the baselines used in the ablative analysis section (4.3) work. Based on this, I do not think this paper is ready for acceptance.

content.title: MonoDETR: Depth-guided Transformer for Monocular 3D Object Detection
content.abstract: Monocular 3D object detection has long been a challenging task in autonomous driving, which requires to decode 3D predictions solely from a single 2D image. Most existing methods follow conventional 2D object detectors to first localize objects based on their centers, and then predict 3D attributes by neighboring features around them. However, only using such local visual features is insufficient to understand the scene-level 3D spatial structures and ignores the long-range inter-object depth relations. In this paper, we introduce a novel framework for Monocular DEtection with a depth-guided TRansformer, named MonoDETR. We modify the vanilla transformer to be depth-aware and guide the whole detection process by contextual depth cues. Specifically, concurrent to the visual encoder that explores object appearances, we specialize a depth encoder to produce the non-local depth embeddings for the scene-level geometric information. Then, we represent 3D object candidates as a set of queries and propose a depth-guided decoder with depth cross-attention modules, which conduct both inter-object and object-scene depth feature interactions. In this way, each object query estimates its 3D attributes adaptively from the depth-guided regions on the image and is no longer constrained to only use local visual features. On KITTI benchmark with monocular images as input, MonoDETR achieves state-of-the-art and requires no extra dense depth annotations. In addition, our depth-guided transformer can also be extended to 3D object detection from multi-view images and show superior performance on nuScenes dataset. Extensive ablation studies have demonstrated the effectiveness of our approach.
